stops.title: The question
stops.text: GPTQ showed us how to shrink weights. SmoothQuant asks the harder question: can we make the activations eight bit too, so the whole matrix multiply runs in integers? That setting is called W eight A eight, eight bit weights and eight bit activations. On large language models it used to break badly. The paper fixes it without any retraining, using only a small calibration set. For the thesis, this is the paper behind the full int8 path in NNCF, as opposed to weight-only compression.

stops.title: Move the difficulty
stops.text: Here is the whole paper in one picture. On the left, a few activation channels are about a hundred times larger than the rest. Weights, by contrast, are smooth and easy. So the idea is to move the difficulty, not change the math. Divide each activation channel by a factor, and multiply the matching weight row by the same factor. The product is exactly the same, but now both sides are comfortable to quantize. Everything else in the paper is about choosing that factor well.

stops.title: Why it breaks
stops.text: Why is this needed at all? Look at this chart of accuracy against model size. With one scale per tensor, or even one scale per token, eight bit activations are fine for small models. From about 6.7 billion parameters on, accuracy collapses to around thirty three percent, close to random guessing. Only a scale per channel stays on the full precision line. That is the key observation: the outliers are not random, they live in a few fixed channels.

stops.title: The hardware catch
stops.text: So why not just scale each activation channel? Because of how an integer matrix multiply works. The sum runs over the input channels inside the kernel, so scales can only be pulled out afterwards along the tokens and the output channels. A per input channel scale would sit inside the sum, and fast int8 kernels cannot do that. Notice the escape hatch in the drawing. The weights are fixed, so the scale can be pushed into them offline, where it costs nothing.

stops.title: One knob called alpha
stops.text: How much difficulty should move? The paper uses one knob, the migration strength alpha. At alpha zero the activations keep all their outliers. At alpha one the weights inherit all of them. In between, the burden is shared. On the paper's toy example, alpha one half turns the worst ratio between channels from eight times into two times, on both sides. For OPT and BLOOM, one half works well. Other models prefer a larger alpha, so it is always worth a quick sweep.

stops.title: Folded away for free
stops.text: Where does the scale actually live at inference time? Nowhere extra. The division is folded into whatever produced the activations, usually the LayerNorm parameters or a previous linear layer. The multiplication goes into the weight rows before they are quantized. So the model runs exactly as before, just with rescaled constants and ordinary int8 kernels. Notice the gold box: when nothing can be folded, NNCF inserts a small explicit multiply instead. That case comes up in LTX-2.3.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: The headline result is on the largest model, OPT with 175 billion parameters. Naive W eight A eight and two earlier methods fall to about thirty six percent, essentially random. SmoothQuant stays within half a point of full precision, just like LLM dot int8, but with pure integer kernels, so it is faster. The paper reports up to 1.56 times speedup and about half the memory. The caveat is alpha: outside roughly 0.4 to 0.6 on this model, accuracy collapses.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what does the thesis take from SmoothQuant? With weight-only int8 or int4, activations are never quantized, and SmoothQuant is not needed at all. If full eight bit activations are tried, NNCF already applies smoothing, so sweep its alpha rather than trusting the default. Calibrate on several prompts times several denoising steps, because ranges drift over time, and expect explicit multiply nodes around the adaptive LayerNorm. Next, AWQ uses the same scaling trick for a different goal, protecting important weights in weight-only int4.
